title: Multimodal content engine
body:
STEM already has decades of applets, simulations, virtual labs, diagrams and teacher-built tools.

AI adds another production route. The useful engine has to understand existing material, generate new objects, keep them editable and check the science.

Questions

  • Which representation should the tutor use for this concept and learner?

  • Can one concept model drive a diagram, animation, simulation and question?

  • How do we preserve meaning when moving between them?

  • Can old Java applets and virtual labs become reusable modern objects?

  • What can be generated during a conversation safely?

  • What needs expert approval?

Output map

  • Text, symbols, derivations, hints

  • Static scientific diagrams

  • Linked equation–graph–diagram views

  • Programmatic animation

  • Interactive diagrams and manipulatives

  • Physics and chemistry simulations

  • Virtual laboratories

  • Learning games

  • 3D and spatial objects

  • Narration and audio

  • Visuals created during tutor dialogue

Several media placed beside one another are still separate assets. Linked representations share objects, variables and state.

Three production paths

Generated media

Text, images, narration, slides and video produced by specialised models.

Google Learn Your Way is useful here. Multi-step workflows; a dedicated educational illustration model; personalisation propagated across outputs.

Generated executable code

Manim, SVG, Canvas, HTML, React or a simulation runtime.

Code gives us objects, parameters and tests. Successful execution says little about the quality of the visual.

Compiled specifications

A declarative learning-object description compiled into one or more renderers.

Vega-Lite, Desmos Computation Layer and the GeoGebra API encode useful parts of this idea.

Working bet

Structured specifications for durable objects. Code generation for unusual objects. Generative media for illustrations, narration and connective material.

Multimodal learning object specification

A possible intermediate representation:

  • Learning intent — objective, prerequisite, misconception, level

  • Entities — named objects, variables, units, identities

  • Model — equations, rules, invariants, boundary conditions

  • Views — diagram, graph, symbolic, particle, 3D

  • Actions — drag, choose, construct, predict, measure

  • State — initial state, transitions, derived values

  • Feedback — conditions, hints, explanations

  • Validation — scientific, behavioural, visual, accessibility

  • Provenance — source, licence, model, prompt, reviewer, corrections

Universal core + subject extensions looks more plausible than one language containing every detail of mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology.

Content primitives

  • Point, vector, path, axis, label, region, constraint

  • Equation, graph, table, proof step, symbolic transform

  • Particle, bond, force, field, ray, circuit component

  • Slider, drag handle, toggle, measurement, checkpoint

  • Predict, compare, construct, debug, balance, optimise

A component library handles rendering. A learning-mechanic library handles what the learner does.

Subject engines

Mathematics

Symbolic equivalence, geometry constraints, plotting, proof structure, exact construction.

Physics

Models, units, numerical integration, initial conditions, invariants, boundary behaviour.

Chemistry

Structures, equations, stoichiometry, microscopic views, lab procedures, safety.

Biology

Annotated structures, scale, process sequences, spatial systems, evidence and variation.

Authoring environment

  • Start from a learning objective, existing asset or rough sketch.

  • Select a representation and mechanic.

  • Edit objects and relationships directly.

  • Point at a visual error and repair its source.

  • Preview representative states.

  • See failed scientific and production checks.

  • Approve a reusable object or family.

SimStep — task-level abstractions and incremental debugging for interactive educational simulations.

ViviDoc — human–agent collaboration for interactive documents.

Generation and repair loop

  1. Interpret learning intent.

  2. Create semantic plan.

  3. Create renderer-specific plan.

  4. Generate specification or code.

  5. Compile and render.

  6. Inspect several states.

  7. Localise the failure.

  8. Repair the smallest responsible part.

  9. Run checks again.

Shared scene state matters. Regenerating each frame or modality independently breaks identity and continuity.

Validation

  • Scientific: equations, units, invariants, topology, solver output

  • Behavioural: transitions, controls, reset, hidden states

  • Visual: overlap, clipping, legibility, hierarchy, continuity

  • Instructional: objective, cognitive load, feedback, useful action

  • Production: schema, dependencies, performance, accessibility

  • Expert: review of science and teaching judgement

SciFlow-Bench — inverse parsing for structure-aware scientific diagram evaluation.

VCG-Bench — structured generation and editing.

Diagram-MMU — multimodal benchmark for scientific diagrams.

SimuScene — code generation for physical scenarios; useful because behaviour across states has to be tested.

Correction memory

Store the failed object, local cause, correction, tests and scope. Reuse only when the same rule applies.

A useful moat may sit here: expert judgement converted into executable checks and reusable production rules.

Existing interactive ecosystems

Brilliant / Diagrammar

Diagrammar talk — reusable abstractions for interactive diagrams.

Hand-crafted, machine-made — generate game content inside an authored mechanic and verification system.

PhET

Open-source HTML5 simulations. Inspect separation of model, view, controls, instrumentation and accessibility.

Open Source Physics / EJS

Open Source Physics and OSP@Singapore expose a large body of models, applets, teacher workflows and migration knowledge.

Javalab

Physics simulations built by an independent developer over many years. Useful corpus for interaction patterns and topic coverage.

Falstad and myPhysicsLab

Falstad applets and myPhysicsLab. Inspect model architecture, licensing and modernisation cost.

Diagramatics

Composable TypeScript diagrams. Small public substrate connecting diagram objects and HTML interaction.

Physics Simulation Engine

Reusable JavaScript simulation runtime. Sits below the instructional layer.

Applet archaeology

  • Run the original safely where possible.

  • Compile or transpile compatible code.

  • Extract entities, equations, controls and states.

  • Rebuild inside a modern component system.

  • Compare behaviour against the original.

  • Add semantic IDs, telemetry and tutor controls.

Existing collections contain production intelligence: which concepts benefit from interaction, useful controls, stable layouts, common edge cases and teacher priorities.

Programmatic animation

Manim gives AI a structured rendering target.

  • Manimator — structured scene description before code.

  • LLM2Manim — pedagogy-aware pipeline, symbol ledger, targeted regeneration and expert review.

  • OmniManim — visual planning, shared scene state and post-render diagnosis.

  • Symbolic Geometric Agent — spatial verification and targeted repair.

  • ManimAgent — reuse of successful reasoning and validated failures.

  • Code2Video — code-centred educational video generation.

Keep the scene model after rendering. The same objects could support pausing, questioning, manipulation and alternate explanations.

Structured diagrams

  • From Text to Visuals — LLM-generated mathematical diagrams as vector graphics.

  • From Words to Structured Visuals — generation and editing benchmark.

  • StarVector — SVG code from images and text.

  • Reason-SVG — structured reasoning for vector generation.

  • VFig — vectorising complex figures into editable SVG.

Tools outside education

  • Figma: agent access to design systems and live project state.

  • Canva: generated code becoming an editable design object.

  • Adobe: orchestration of specialised models inside production workflows.

  • Unity: AI operating against a live project and executable runtime.

  • Roblox: generation through schemas, then behaviour.

  • NVIDIA Omniverse: simulation-ready assets and physical constraints.

  • Autodesk Fusion: options generated inside engineering constraints.

  • Houdini: procedural dependency graphs.

  • OpenUSD: layered scene composition without flattening ownership.

  • BioRender: domain-specific libraries and scientific conventions.

  • World Labs / Runway: spatial and visual identity across generated scenes.

Possible architectures

  1. Media factory — coordinated generators for familiar formats.

  2. Code-production agent — plan, generate, render, inspect, repair.

  3. Component composer — assemble approved primitives and mechanics.

  4. Educational compiler — semantic learning object compiled to renderers.

  5. Simulation federation — registry over existing verified engines.

  6. Hybrid — compiler, component system, code agent and media models.

Runtime inside the tutor

  1. Retrieve an approved object.

  2. Parameterise a verified family.

  3. Compose approved components.

  4. Generate inside a constrained runtime.

  5. Fall back to a static verified representation.

The tutor needs event outputs: what the learner changed, predicted, measured, tried and misunderstood.

Opportunity map

  • Applet archaeologist — discover, classify and modernise legacy STEM interactives.

  • STEM scene compiler — subject objects, relationships and renderers.

  • Interactive-courseware copilot — expert authoring and direct repair.

  • Simulation registry — instructional search and tutor-callable tools.

  • Validator — tests and benchmarks for generated STEM media.

  • Content-family generator — verified variants with difficulty control.

  • Multimodal object compiler — shared semantics across representations.

  • EduReady pipeline — add semantics, controls and telemetry to ordinary assets.

Experiments

  • Raw code vs a small STEM DSL across several concepts.

  • Migrate twelve applets from different technical eras.

  • One model rendered as diagram, animation, simulation and game.

  • Physics state explorer that searches for hidden failures.

  • Click a visual error and trace it to the semantic source.

  • Generate a hundred verified variants from one mechanic.

  • Retrieve simulations by instructional affordance.

  • Replay an expert correction on related objects.

Evidence to save with a demo

  • Input and intermediate representations

  • Number of generations and manual edits

  • Model, prompt and component versions

  • Execution and validation results

  • States and edge cases tested

  • Expert review status

  • Rights and provenance

  • Time to draft and approval

  • Editability and reliable variant generation

Moat?

  • Intermediate representation

  • Subject primitives and mechanics

  • Verified content families

  • Expert correction memory

  • Failure benchmarks

  • Applet and simulation registry

  • Cross-modal production graph

  • Learner interaction data tied to content decisions

Open loops

  • Where should the universal representation end?

  • Which subject gets the first compiler?

  • How should instructional affordances be indexed?

  • Can AI infer equations and hidden state from an old applet?

  • Which corrections generalise safely?

  • How much generation is acceptable during live tutoring?

  • What predicts expert rejection?

  • How do we measure learning value separately from visual appeal?

  • Licensing for legacy and community-built material.

  • Accessibility across diagrams, interaction, animation and audio.

Strongest combined bet

  • Retrieval and archaeology layer

  • Semantic STEM compiler

  • Expert production copilot

  • Validation and tutor runtime
